p1orig = alt.Chart(college).mark_circle(opacity=0.5, size=40).encode(
    alt.X('AcceptanceRate:Q',
          title='Acceptance Rate(%)',
          scale=alt.Scale(domain=[100,0])),
    alt.Y('Top10HS:Q',
          title='% Students from Top 10% of High School Class')
).transform_calculate(
    AcceptanceRate = 'datum.Accepted/datum.Applied * 100'
).properties(
    width=500,
    height=300,
    title='Acceptance Rate vs % Students in Top 10% of High School Class'
)

p1updated = alt.Chart(college).mark_circle(opacity=0.5, size=40).encode(
    alt.X('AcceptanceRate:Q',
          title='Acceptance Rate(%)',
          scale=alt.Scale(domain=[100,0])),
    alt.Y('Top10HS:Q',
          title='% Students from Top 10% of High School Class')
).transform_calculate(
    AcceptanceRate = 'datum.Accepted/datum.Applied * 100'
).properties(
    width=500,
    height=300,
    title=alt.Title(
        "Acceptance Rate vs % Students in Top 10% of High School Class",
        subtitle=[" Schools with lower acceptnce rates tend to enroll",
                  "a higher proportion of students from the top 10% of their high school class."],
        anchor='start',
        frame='group',
        orient='bottom',
        offset=15
    )
)

Step 2: Explore the Data¶

Explore the data by considering the following questions:

  • How many unique names are there?
  • Pick one name that might have multiple spellings. Are there similar names that are spelled differently? Use fuzzy matching to see which names might be similar.
  • How many names does each pet have? Is there a pattern you can pull out from that?
  • Do any names stand out to you? For example, are there patterns in using certian prefixes to names, or name endings?
  • Are there any common terms used in the breeds of the pets?

You are welcome to explore other patterns as well!

Leave all your exploration steps here to show what you looked at, but be sure to clean up your code to show a final version of each exploration.

In [32]:
# How many unique names are there?
print("Unique names:", pets['animal_s_name'].nunique())

# Fuzzy matching - find names similar to "Bella"
all_names = pets['animal_s_name'].dropna().unique().tolist()
print("\nFuzzy matches for 'Bella':")
print(process.extract("Bella", all_names, limit=5))

# How many words does each pet name have?
print("\nName word count distribution:")
print(pets['name_count'].value_counts().sort_index())

# Prefix patterns using str.contains()
prefixes = ['Mr', 'Princess', 'Sir', 'Lady', 'King', 'Queen', 'Captain']
print("\nPrefix counts:")
for p in prefixes:
    count = pets['animal_s_name'].str.contains(p, case=False, na=False).sum()
    print(f"  {p}: {count}")

# Extract the prefix from names using str.extract()
print("\nExtracted prefixes:")
print(pets['animal_s_name'].str.extract('(^Mr|^Princess|^Sir|^Lady|^King|^Queen|^Captain)').dropna())

# Common breed terms
print("\nDomestic breeds:", pets['primary_breed'].str.contains('Domestic', na=False).sum())
print("Mix breeds:", pets['primary_breed'].str.contains('Mix', na=False).sum())

Step 3: Make a Plot¶

Pick an interesting patterns that you found in your exploration above. Make a well-considered plot of this pattern. It does not need to be groundbreaking, but make sure it uses some kind of text manipulation from the above data. It should not be a word cloud but a regular Altair graphic (line, bar, scatterplot, etc).

What one-sentence conclusion should we draw from this plot?

STUDENT RESPONSE

"Mr." is the most popular formal title given to Seattle pets, appearing more than twice as often as the next most common title "Sir."

In [33]:
# Extract the prefix from names using str.extract() - directly from demo
pets['prefix'] = pets['animal_s_name'].str.extract('(Mr|Princess|Sir|Lady|King|Queen|Captain)')
prefix_counts = pets['prefix'].value_counts().reset_index()
prefix_counts.columns = ['prefix', 'count']


# Plot which royal/formal titles are most common in pet names
alt.Chart(prefix_counts).mark_bar().encode(
    alt.X('prefix:N', title='Name Title/Prefix', axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
    alt.Y('count:Q', title='Number of Pets'),
    alt.Color('prefix:N', legend=None)
).properties(
    width=400,
    height=300,
    title='Which Formal Titles Are Most Popular in Seattle Pet Names?'
)
Out[33]:

Step 4: Perfect and Save Your Plot¶

Take your plot from above and make it beautiful. Add a descriptive title, subtitle, and axes labels. Edit the fonts and styles to be attractive and well-sized. Add alt-text using the description argument and make sure it describes the data behind the plot.

final_chart = alt.Chart(prefix_counts).mark_bar().encode(
    alt.X('prefix:N',
          title='Name Title/Prefix',
          axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
    alt.Y('count:Q',
          title='Number of Pets'),
    alt.Color('prefix:N', legend=None)
).properties(
    width=400,
    height=300,
    title=alt.Title(
        "Formal Titles in Seattle Pet Names",
        subtitle=["'Mr.' is the most popular formal title for pets,",
                  "followed by 'Sir' and 'Captain'."],
        anchor='start',
        frame='group',
        orient='bottom',
        offset=15
    ),
    description="Bar chart showing how frequently each formal title such as Mr., Sir, Princess, Captain appears in Seattle pet names. Mr. is the most common."
).configure_axis(
    titleFontSize=14,
    labelFontSize=12
).configure_view(
    stroke=None
)

final_chart.save('pet_titles.png')
